newsitem.title: UK: Minor metals - Russian cobalt up, vanadium stirs.
newsitem.headline: Minor metals - Russian cobalt up, vanadium stirs.

text.p: Little movement was seen in most minor metals over the past week apart from Russian cobalt which snapped higher on consumer demand.
Elsewhere, vanadium firmed on a lack of available material while silicon prices slipped under Chinese offers.
Traders said despite the onset of the traditionally slow summer period consumer demand lifted Russian cobalt.
"Usually there is enough material on the ground to satisfy the needs of consumers during the summer period...the market looks to have been caught short," one trader said.
Traders said that a large U.K. based chemical company was looking to buy around 50 tonnes of cobalt, but did not disclose the time period which the purchase would cover.
"At the moment the consumer is helping to cap the market after only buying small amounts, believing that prices are running too high," a trader said.
Other traders said that the recent pricing operation that has pressured prices lower has now bottomed out.
"We seem to be in the first stage of a recovery following the recent slide...July/August may see the market around current levels, though I expect prices to rise on demand in September," one said.
Any signs of fresh consumer covering could move prices to $25 a pound given tight market fundamentals, another said.

A trade source with contacts in Russia said that producers in the region were not willing to move large amounts of material after the recent downside pricing operation. "They seem to be holding off in anticipation of a rise in prices," the trade source said.
Traders noted news that the U.S. Defense National Stockpile Center planned to offer for sale 500,000 pounds of cobalt in August and intends a further 1.5 million pound sale in September.
Cobalt sales were suspended in March following a legal dispute between the Stockpile and trader Minor Metals Inc.
Traders opinions varied of the impact of the resumption of the sales which has left the market starved of Stockpile material for three months.

One trader suggested that the material could help to meet consumer demand and push the market lower. Others disagreed saying the market would remain stable as the Stockpile will not make up the short fall of suspended sales.
"The DLA is not going to flood the market...their total sales for the fiscal year ending in September will be far short of the six million tonnes they could have sold," a trader said.

A shortage of spot material firmed vanadium. Traders said that producers China and Russian were running low stock levels in a market already suffering from a lack of South African material following recent heavy rains which have affected production.
Chinese selling and low demand saw silicon drift lower. Traders said with few signs of consumer demand on the horizon they expect prices to fall further.
Offers out of China kept antimony under pressure and several traders are expecting a further easing amid the slow summer conditions.
